week.t: NASA: Artemis III becomes a rehearsal, landings move to 2028
Swift telescope retires after 22 years and 2,000 explosions
Dragonfly flies its first simulated flight for Titan
Nobel week: ghost particles, light-switch neurons

tiles.cap: NASA just rewrote the Moon plan. Artemis III won't land. It will rehearse.
tiles.p1: On Friday NASA announced that Artemis III, launching in 2027, stays in Earth orbit: Orion docks with a Blue Origin test lander, then a SpaceX Starship test ship, to check every system before anyone tries the surface.
tiles.p2: The actual landings near the Moon's south pole are now set for 2028.
deep: Three rockets, one mission

Blue Origin's Blue Moon test lander launches first into a 273-mile orbit, where it can wait up to 30 days. Orion follows on SLS days later, climbs to about 345 miles, and after two days of checks docks with it. The crew spends about two days inside, testing the cabin, controls and life support.
Then Starship

SpaceX launches a Starship Version 3 test article into a lower orbit. Orion docks with it for up to two hours. Nobody goes aboard; the point is to prove the two ships can find each other, talk, and hold together.
Who flies

Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas and ESA's Luca Parmitano. After the dockings they have up to five more days for spacesuit checks, sensor tests and experiments, then splash down off California.
Why rehearse
Docking a crew capsule to a lander the size of a building has never been done. Doing it 345 miles up, where a problem means coming home in hours, is cheaper than finding out 240,000 miles away.

tiles.cap: Why Moon rovers can't run on solar panels
tiles.nums: of darkness in every lunar night
tiles.p1: A night on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks and the temperature drops to around minus 170 °C. Solar panels give nothing and ordinary batteries freeze. NASA's Moon-base rovers are being built around small nuclear power modules that give steady heat and electricity through the dark.
tiles.p2: NASA posted a progress update on these rovers this week.
deep: What the module does
A radioisotope power system uses the heat from a slowly decaying element to make electricity and to keep the rover's insides warm. No moving parts, no sunlight needed, and it runs for years.
Same trick, other worlds
Curiosity and Perseverance on Mars run on the same idea, which is why they drive through dust storms that would kill a solar rover. Voyager 1 and 2 have been running on it since 1977.
Why the south pole

That is where the 2028 landings aim. Some crater floors there have not seen sunlight in billions of years and hold water ice; some crater rims are lit almost all the time. The base goes between the two.

tiles.cap: Astronomers found the first green star
tiles.p1: Stars are supposed to be red, orange, yellow, white or blue, never green, because of how our eyes mix the colours a hot object gives off. A team at the University of Warwick found a dead star, WD J1330+6435, that would look green to a human eye.
tiles.p2: NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day featured it on Wednesday.
deep: Why stars are never green

A star glows across the whole rainbow at once. A star peaking in green also pours out plenty of red and blue, and your eye adds them up to white. That is why the Sun, which peaks in green, looks white from space.
How this one cheats

WD J1330+6435 is a white dwarf, the leftover core of a Sun-like star. It has been swallowing rocky debris, and those trace elements in its atmosphere absorb some colours and let others through. The filtered light that escapes reads as green.
A rainbow of dead stars

The same survey found white dwarfs that would look yellow, cyan, pink and purple. Each colour is a fingerprint of what the star has eaten, which tells astronomers what the planets around it were made of.

tiles.cap: A telescope built to last 2 years just retired after 22. It caught 2,000 explosions.
tiles.nums: gamma-ray bursts caught by Swift since 2004
tiles.p1: Gamma-ray bursts are the most powerful explosions known, and they last seconds. Swift's job was to notice one, swing round in under a minute, and stare. It did that for more than 2,000 of them before its orbit sank too low to hold steady. Its last observation was on 20 October.
tiles.p2: It will burn up in Earth's atmosphere in the coming weeks.
deep: The 0.03-second catch

In May 2005 a burst lasted three hundredths of a second. Swift turned fast enough to catch 11 X-ray photons of its afterglow, the first ever for a short burst. That is how we learned short bursts come from two neutron stars colliding.
Why it is falling
At under 275 km up there is still a whisper of air. Over 22 years that drag pulled Swift down until the telescope could no longer hold its aim. There was no engine to boost it back up.
What it leaves
1,400 supernovae, stars seen being torn apart by black holes, about 7,000 scientific papers and 12 terabytes of public data anyone can use.

tiles.cap: NASA's car-sized drone for Saturn's moon just flew its first simulated flight
tiles.nums: arrival at Titan after a six-year cruise
tiles.p1: Dragonfly is a rotorcraft that will hop across Titan, the only moon with a thick atmosphere and the only other place with rivers and lakes, made of liquid methane. On Thursday engineers ran its entire first flight on the real flight computers: drop from the heat shield, scan the dunes, pick a safe spot, land.
tiles.p2: Launch no earlier than 2028. Titan is too far for anyone to steer it, so it decides for itself.
deep: Why a drone works there

Titan's air is four times denser than Earth's and gravity is one seventh. Flying is easier than on Earth; the same rotor lifts far more. On Mars, with air 1% as thick, the Ingenuity helicopter could barely lift itself.
Deciding alone
Radio to Titan takes over an hour each way. Dragonfly uses cameras, motion sensors and lidar to measure slope and spot hazards, then chooses where to land, like Perseverance's AutoNav but in the air.
What it is looking for
Titan's chemistry resembles early Earth's before life. Dragonfly will sample the sand and ice at many sites over three years to see how far that chemistry got.

tiles.cap: Mosquitoes pick their victims by smell. Each species likes a different person.
tiles.nums: volunteers sniffed by three mosquito species
tiles.p1: Researchers at Florida International University let three mosquito species smell 119 people's arms through a cage. Each species had its own favourites. Some people drew two species. Nobody drew all three.
tiles.p2: Singapore's dengue mosquito, Aedes aegypti, went for people with less skin odour, not more.
deep: How they tested it

Day-biting Aedes mosquitoes sniffed arms in the lab through a device that blocked biting. Night-biting Culex got nylon sleeves the volunteers had worn for hours. The team also sampled the chemicals in the air around each arm and swabbed the skin for bacteria.
What each species wanted
Aedes aegypti and Culex preferred people with weaker overall odour. Aedes albopictus, the tiger mosquito, was drawn to 13 plant-like chemicals. Certain skin bacteria attracted all three.
Why it matters here

Dengue cases track Aedes aegypti. If skin bacteria make the attractive smells, a repellent could work by changing your skin's microbes, and the attractive chemicals could bait traps instead of people.

tiles.cap: Satellites say this El Niño now rivals the monster of 1997
tiles.nums: chance it stays strong into early 2027 (NOAA)
tiles.p1: NASA put 2026's ocean next to 1997 and 2015 using 35 years of sea-height measurements. The shape matches 1997: a tilt of warm, high water stretching to South America. This one arrived faster, and JPL's Josh Willis says it is on track to be even bigger.
tiles.p2: 1997-98 brought floods to California and drought and fire to Southeast Asia.
deep: Measuring heat with a ruler
Warm water expands. Satellites that bounce radar off the sea can measure its height to a few centimetres, so a bulge in the eastern Pacific is a direct reading of stored heat.
Three satellites, one record
TOPEX/Poseidon measured 1997, Jason-2 measured 2015, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich measures now. They fly almost the same track, so the maps compare cleanly.
What it means for us
For Singapore the pattern is drier, hotter, hazier. The haze tile on this wall is the first instalment.

tiles.cap: Saturday was the worst haze day so far. Today should ease.
tiles.p1: Southeasterly winds carried smoke from fires in Sumatra and Borneo straight over Singapore on Saturday. For today NEA forecasts PSI of 80 to 130 as winds swing to the southwest, and showers over the weekend and into Monday should bring it down further.
tiles.p2: The fires are in peat: ancient plant matter that smoulders underground for weeks.
deep: Reading the numbers
PSI tracks fine particles 2.5 microns across, a thirtieth of a hair's width. Below 50 is Good, 51 to 100 Moderate, 101 to 200 Unhealthy. Above 100 the advice is to cut long runs and sport outdoors.
Why wind direction is everything
The fires did not change between Friday and Saturday. The wind did. From the northeast, smoke misses us. From the southeast, it arrives in hours.
The bigger engine
A dry season this severe is the El Niño on this wall. NOAA gives it an 83% chance of staying strong into 2027, so expect repeats until the rains return.

tiles.cap: NUS wove a touchscreen into a sleeve. It goes in the wash.
tiles.p1: Each fibre carries 96 LEDs and senses touch at the same time. Over 5,000 chips are linked by 20,000+ connections, all pulled through a thermal drawing process like making glass fibre. Published in Nature on 22 October.
tiles.p2: First use: a sleeve that shows your body temperature. Led by Asst Prof Tural Khudiyev.
deep: How you make a glowing thread

Start with a thick rod containing the LEDs and wires, heat it, and pull it into a long thin fibre, the same thermal drawing used to make fibre-optic cable. Each fibre ends up with 96 tiny LEDs along it and can sense a fingertip.
Then weave it
54 of those fibres go into ordinary fabric to make a 96 by 54 pixel screen, 168 by 105 mm, on a sleeve. Over 5,000 chips, more than 20,000 connections, and it survives the washing machine.
What it's for

Clothing that shows your temperature or heart rate, or acts as a controller for your phone, without a separate device. Led by Assistant Professor Tural Khudiyev at NUS; published in Nature on 22 October 2026.

tiles.cap: Singapore is sending an AI into orbit the size of a shoebox
tiles.p1: Singapore's space programme is building three satellites to launch in 2026, 2027 and 2028. One runs small AI models in orbit so it sends down answers, not raw photos, and tests perovskite solar cells in space for the first time.
tiles.p2: Another carries a Singapore-built electric engine that can raise or lower a satellite's orbit.
deep: The plan
Singapore's Office for Space Technology and Industry is funding three satellites, one launch a year in 2026, 2027 and 2028, built with NTU and local companies.
Satellite one

A 3-unit cubesat, 30 by 10 by 10 cm, that runs small AI models on board to analyse its own photos in orbit and only sends down the useful parts. It also carries perovskite solar cells, a cheaper, lighter kind never before tested in space.
Satellite two

A 16-unit, 30 kg craft with an electric engine from NTU spin-off Aliena that can raise or lower its orbit, plus a detector for atomic oxygen, the corrosive gas that eats spacecraft in very low orbits.
Satellite three
A camera from LightHaus Photonics, tested on the International Space Station, built to pick out objects about a metre across from orbit.

tiles.cap: A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice is the world's biggest telescope
tiles.nums: neutrinos through your fingernail every second
tiles.p1: Neutrinos fly straight through planets without noticing. IceCube buried 5,000 light sensors in South Pole ice and waits for the rare one that hits an atom and flashes. It caught neutrinos from black holes billions of light-years away.
tiles.p2: Why now: it won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics on 6 October.
deep: How you see a particle that touches nothing

Neutrinos barely interact, so you need a huge amount of stuff for one to hit. IceCube uses a cubic kilometre of clear ice as the target. When a neutrino finally smacks an atom, it kicks off a charged particle that moves faster than light does in ice and gives off a faint blue glow, which the buried sensors catch.
Why the South Pole

Ice at 1.5 to 2.5 km down is some of the clearest material on Earth, it is already there for free, and it is dark. The sensors were lowered down holes melted with hot water and have been frozen in place since 2010.
What it found

Neutrinos with millions of times the energy of anything our accelerators make, arriving from a flaring galaxy 4 billion light-years away and from our own Milky Way. We can now point at the sky and ask what is firing them, with a messenger nothing can block.
The person
Francis Halzen, 82, born in Belgium, a theorist at the University of Wisconsin who had the idea in the 1980s and spent 30 years getting it built. Physics Nobel 2026, awarded on 6 October.

tiles.cap: A Mars robot just set the off-world driving record. It drove itself.
tiles.p1: Perseverance beat Opportunity's 8-year record in half the time. 90% of it was self-driven: radio to Earth takes up to 20 minutes, so no human can steer live.
tiles.p2: Same problem NASA's Moon-base rovers are being designed around right now.
deep: Why it can't be driven from Earth

A radio signal takes 4 to 20 minutes to reach Mars depending on where the planets are. By the time a driver on Earth saw a rock, the rover would already have hit it. So drives are planned in the morning and the rover executes them alone.
How AutoNav works

While rolling, the rover photographs the ground ahead in stereo, builds a 3D map, scores every patch for danger, picks a path, and repeats, several times a minute. Opportunity could do a crude version about 5% of the time. Perseverance does it 90% of the time and drives up to 412 metres in a day.
The record
45.22 km on 11 October 2026, beating Opportunity's 45.16 km, set over 14 years. Perseverance did it in under six. NASA has extended its mission to the end of 2028.
What it's doing out there
Climbing the rim of Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed, collecting rock cores in sealed tubes that a future mission is meant to bring back to Earth.

tiles.cap: An AI proved a cousin of the hardest problem in maths
tiles.p1: The Riemann hypothesis is a 167-year-old question about how primes are spread. On 6 October an AI settled the "quasi-Riemann hypothesis", a softer version, and human experts have checked it.
tiles.p2: Mathematicians are split between "staggering" and "what's left for us?"
deep: The problem
Primes look random, but the Riemann hypothesis says their spacing follows a hidden pattern tied to a function called zeta. Proving it has resisted everyone since 1859 and carries a $1 million prize.
What the AI did

On 6 October OpenAI released hundreds of machine-written papers. One proved the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a strictly weaker statement that still says a lot about primes. Earlier AI claims had holes; this one has been checked line by line by mathematicians at Stanford and elsewhere and stands.
Why mathematicians are rattled

Some call it the biggest AI-for-maths result so far. Others ask what a mathematician's job is if machines can find and prove deep results. Quanta ran a piece titled 'Is AI the end of math as we know it?'
Your angle
Olympiad-style problems are now routine for these systems. The skills that still matter are choosing which question to ask and knowing when a proof is beautiful rather than merely correct.

tiles.cap: Stare at this and your eyes will invent a colour
tiles.p1: Your three colour sensors tire out separately. Wear out green, look at white, and you see a magenta ghost. That's an afterimage.
tiles.p2: Then mix red, green and blue light yourself in the PhET simulator.
deep: What's happening in your eye

Your retina has three kinds of cone cells, roughly for red, green and blue. Stare at one colour and the cones for it get fatigued and fire less. Look at white, and the other two shout louder, so you see the opposite colour.
The test
Look at the white dot in the green disc for 30 seconds without moving your eyes. Then look at a blank white wall. You should see a magenta disc that follows your gaze and fades over several seconds.
Try variations
Stare at red and you see cyan. Stare at blue and you see yellow. Half-cover the shape and the ghost has a hard edge. Blink and it jumps.
Mix light yourself
Red + green light = yellow. All three = white. Your screen does this with every pixel.

tiles.cap: Pond algae gave scientists a light switch for brain cells
tiles.p1: An alga steers toward light with a protein that opens like a gate under blue light. Put that gene in a neuron, shine a light, the neuron fires on command.
tiles.p2: Memory, fear, sleep and tremors are all being mapped this way. 2026 Nobel in Medicine.
deep: The trick

Neurons fire when charged atoms rush through gates in their membrane. Channelrhodopsin, a protein from a pond alga, is a gate that opens when blue light hits it. Insert its gene into a neuron and you have a cell that fires whenever you flash it.
Who did what

Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel found and decoded the algal protein. Karl Deisseroth, a psychiatrist and engineer at Stanford, got it working in brain cells in 2005 and built the tools to use it in living animals.
Why it's a big deal

Before this you could only stimulate a lump of brain with electricity. Now you can switch one exact type of cell on or off with millisecond timing and watch what changes: a memory, a craving, a tremor.
Already in people
Light-sensitive proteins have been put into the eyes of a blind patient, who regained partial vision. Medicine Nobel 2026, awarded 5 October.
